Next month's 26th marks the first anniversary of the Tai Po Wang Fuk Court fire. The independent committee investigating the fire is expected to submit a report to the Chief Executive before the end of October. Recent reports indicated that the government has activated the Head of Department Accountability System to investigate the administrative responsibility for the fire and has re-deployed administrative officers to assist. Chief Executive John Lee today (the 6th) did not respond as to whether the mechanism has been activated, stating that the government has made a series of deployments and will implement reforms and pursue accountability as soon as possible after the report is submitted. The luxury residence One Stanley in Stanley was exposed to have reinforcing steel that did not match the plans. Lee stated that the Buildings Department is investigating the case and has requested the Development Bureau to oversee the investigation. As multiple projects have been exposed to problems one after another, he said he attaches importance to the construction quality of Hong Kong's building projects, which relates to the professional standards, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and the government will strictly enforce the law.

The Wang Fuk Court fire is approaching its one-year mark, and the independent committee is expected to submit a report before the end of October. (File photo)

Earlier media reports stated that two administrative officers, former Deputy Secretary for Security Mok Kwan-yu and Commissioner for Sports Choi Kin-fan, would provide support at an investigation小组 under the Public Service Commission, specifically tasked with preliminary work on administrative accountability.

Chief Executive John Lee attended a press conference before the Executive Council meeting today and was asked whether the matter was true? With the activation of the Head of Department Accountability System to investigate responsibility, does it mean that even if there is a report, any matters involving official accountability will not have immediate results, and how long must the public wait?

Lee stated that he made it clear from the start that after the independent committee submits the report, he will actively study and follow up on recommendations, implement reforms and announce details. He did not directly respond as to whether administrative officers have already been redeployed to prepare preliminary investigation work, only saying that "the government has made a series of deployments during this period," emphasising that after the report is submitted, based on its content, he will "implement comprehensive reforms and pursue accountability as soon as possible in the short term," with detailed announcements to follow.

Lee stated that after the independent committee submits the report, reforms and accountability will be pursued as soon as possible based on the report's content. (File photo)

Lee also reiterated multiple times that improvement measures are urgent, so when the Policy Address was delivered in September, seven priority improvement measures were announced, including banning smoking on construction sites, strengthening regulation of fire service installations, enhancing disciplinary action and punishment against professionals and contractors, improving compliance in owners' corporations, studying the criminalisation of bid-rigging, providing tendering and evaluation services for the first time, establishing prequalification lists for consultants and contractors, and researching solutions to better assist the public with projects involving professional expertise.

According to records, the Public Service Commission is an independent statutory advisory body that advises the Chief Executive on civil service appointments, promotions and disciplinary matters. The Head of Department Accountability System was proposed by Chief Executive John Lee in last year's Policy Address, establishing a two-tier investigation mechanism based on the severity of departmental issues. If the issue is less serious in nature or involves an isolated incident, the first-tier investigation will be conducted by the head of department. If the department has serious problems, or involves extensive, recurring systemic issues, or may involve the role of the head of department, a second-tier investigation will be launched by an investigation小组 led by the Public Service Commission.

The luxury residence One Stanley was exposed to have units where the reinforcing steel did not match the plans. Lee said he would not comment on cases still under investigation and has requested the Development Bureau to oversee the Buildings Department's investigation.

One Stanley 'rebars problematic' – Development Bureau requested to oversee investigation

Recently, one construction project after another has been exposed to problems, including the lift shaft tilt at the new block of Queen Mary Hospital, concrete samples at a Tung Chung public housing estate not meeting strength standards, and reinforcing steel in floor slabs at the Stanley luxury residence One Stanley not matching the plans. Lee was asked whether there are problems with construction and even project supervision?

He responded to the One Stanley project issue, stating that the Buildings Department is seriously investigating the case, "to ascertain whether construction quality and supervision were adequate, and will handle it strictly in accordance with the law." As the investigation is still ongoing, he would not comment on the case details, and has requested the Development Bureau to oversee the case investigation. However, he emphasised that he attaches importance to the construction quality of Hong Kong's building projects, "paying attention to whether professionals related to the project have diligently supervised, and whether contractors have violated regulations during construction," and noted that this concerns the professional standards, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and the government will inevitably strictly enforce the law.

He has also requested the Development Bureau to enhance regulatory requirements and penalties in terms of legislation for construction projects as a whole, to ensure the deterrent effect of the law, severely punish relevant personnel in violation, and safeguard the professional standards, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction projects. The Development Bureau will submit proposed amendments to the Buildings Ordinance this year to strengthen regulation and enhance the penalty system and sanctions, and the authorities will push forward the related work at full speed.

The difficulty faced by nursing graduates in finding jobs has recently attracted attention. Lee stated that there is a long-term demand for nurses, and pointed out that the Hospital Authority currently has over 3,000 nursing vacancies that graduates may apply for. (File photo)

Executive Councillor Tommy Cheung criticises 'unions impersonating people' – Lee states demand exists long-term

Discussions about nurses' difficulty in finding jobs have heated up recently. The source was a radio phone-in programme after the Policy Address, where a Mr. Kwok, who claimed to be a psychiatric nurse in a disciplinary force, said his application for deferred retirement was not approved, and that his daughter, a nursing graduate, was unemployed immediately upon graduation, questioning the Hospital Authority's recruitment of Mainland medical and nursing staff. Executive Councillor Tommy Cheung subsequently questioned whether it was the unions "possibly impersonating people making phone calls," and expressed his wholehearted support for importing foreign talent.

Reporters asked about the difficulty faced by nursing graduates in finding jobs, how to address the concentration of vacancies in experienced nurses? How to respond to Executive Councillor remarks that are said to aggravate social conflicts? Lee stated that in every industry, there are cases where graduates do not seek employment immediately after graduation for individual reasons, or where recruiting institutions select those most suitable for their needs, "resulting in cases where certain individuals are not hired." He emphasised that the society's demand for nurses has always existed, especially with Hong Kong's continuous medical development and the trend of population ageing, "so recruitment numbers will ultimately inevitably reflect these existing demands." He also pointedly noted that "there are different discussions in society on this aspect, which allows everyone to discuss the issue more clearly."

Lee also stated that based on 2025/26 figures, there are approximately 4,000 potential nursing graduates, with about 2,500 actually applying to the Hospital Authority, meaning 1,500 have applied for positions outside the Hospital Authority, and the Hospital Authority currently still has over 3,000 nursing vacancies, "nursing graduates can apply, and there is a chance of being hired."

Secretary for Health Professor Lo Chung-mau earlier accepted interviews with multiple media outlets to clarify that the government's recruitment policy definitely prioritises local talent. Lee also reiterated that based on the current number of nurses in the Hospital Authority, "99.8% are locally trained Hong Kong nurses," clearly implementing the policy of prioritising local talent in employment. He also pointed out that currently 40% of nurses work in the public healthcare system, with the remaining 60% in other medical positions, such as community nursing, elderly care, rehabilitation services, and private medical institutions. He emphasised that there is a long-term societal demand for nurses. The government will, in accordance with healthcare service needs, exchange views with the industry and academia, and plan well for medical and nursing training and manpower development.
